items.title: 8 AI model architectures, visually explained:
items.summary:
8 AI model architectures, visually explained:

LLMs get so much attention that it's easy to overlook the rest of the field. Different inputs, tasks, and deployment constraints have led to very different model designs.

Here are eight specialized AI model architectures:

1. LLM (Large language models)

Text is split into tokens, mapped to embeddings, and processed through transformer layers. The model generates its response by predicting successive tokens.

↳ GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.

2. LCM (Large concept models)

Moves prediction to the sentence level. Sentences become SONAR embeddings, and the model predicts the next sentence representation. Meta explored both autoregressive and diffusion-based versions.

↳ Meta's LCM research introduced this approach.

3. LAM (Large action models)

Connects a user's request to actions in an environment. These systems interpret intent, plan steps, and use interfaces or tools, often checking results before continuing.

↳ Rabbit R1, Microsoft UFO, Claude Computer Use.

4. MoE (Mixture of experts)

A router assigns token representations to selected expert networks inside the model. Activating a subset of experts adds model capacity without running every expert for every token.

↳ Mixtral, DeepSeek, Switch Transformer.

5. VLM (Vision-language models)

Combines visual representations with language processing. A vision encoder extracts image features, which are connected to a language model so it can answer questions about visual content.

↳ GPT-4V, Gemini, LLaVA.

6. SLM (Small language models)

Uses fewer parameters to reduce memory and compute requirements. These models can run locally, with quantization often reducing their deployment footprint further.

↳ Phi-3, Gemma, Mistral 7B, Llama 3.2 1B.

7. MLM (Masked language models)

Learns by predicting hidden tokens using context on both sides. This bidirectional training produces representations useful for retrieval, classification, and other language-understanding tasks.

↳ BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa.

8. SAM (Segment Anything Model)

An image encoder processes the image, while a prompt encoder handles points, boxes, or masks. A mask decoder combines them to identify the requested regions.

↳ Meta's SAM supports interactive segmentation and image annotation.

These aren't eight mutually exclusive categories. A small model can process images, and a language model can use MoE layers. Some labels describe architecture, while others describe training or intended use.

There's another approach I kept outside the image because it alters how a model handles context rather than introducing a separate model family.

Recursive language models, from MIT, put the input into a Python environment that a root model can inspect through code.

The model can search or slice that input, then make recursive model calls on selected portions instead of loading everything into its own context window.

The reported experiments handled inputs beyond 10 million tokens without retraining, with gains over the base model even on some tasks whose inputs already fit its context window.

I recently wrote a full breakdown of how this works, including why accessing a large input and reasoning reliably over it are different problems.

Read it below.

items.title: ONE token turned a $0.40 AI request into $0.80.
items.summary:
ONE token turned a $0.40 AI request into $0.80.

and 4 "cheap" $20 subscriptions quietly cost $1,080 a year.

so i wrote 98 lines of python to audit what AI actually costs. real published prices, no vibes.

it said cut $360. the cache line alone was -88%.

here's what nobody checks.

ChatGPT Plus $20. Claude Pro $20. SuperGrok $30. Cursor Pro $20.
$90 a month. $1,080 a year. before tax.

each one looks reasonable the day you click subscribe. the bill only shows up when they stack

what the script printed, prices as of Aug 28, US web:

> 5M input + 1M output tokens a month: Sonnet 5 $20.00, Grok 4.6 $16.00, GPT-5.6 Luna $2.20
> use 1/5 of that and Sonnet is $4. not $20
> keep 2 subs + a $20 API budget: $720/yr. saves $360
> agent sending the same 100K prompt 50 times: $10.00 naive, $1.23 cached. -88%
> batch API: half price if you can wait
> Grok 4.6 at 199,999 tokens: $0.40. at 200,000: $0.80. one token doubles the whole request
> 20K records to JSON: $160 on Sol, $8.80 on Luna (my assumption: 1K in / 200 out each)

the lesson isn't "API is cheaper". heavy users burn $20 of API in days. the lesson is most people never did the math

how to audit yours:
1. list every AI sub and what you actually use it for
2. split the product (IDE, bots, connectors) from the model access
3. log 30 days of how often you open each one
4. move the occasional ones to pay-per-token
5. cache stable prompts, batch what can wait, watch the 200K / 272K cliffs
6. route easy work to cheap models, keep the frontier one for hard problems

every subscription has to earn its spot on your card. my math on published prices, not financial advice

# AI and your job: Threat or opportunity?

Artificial intelligence is changing the workplace. Learn how it could affect jobs and where to find AI training in Alabama.

By Lenise Ligon

Published: Nov. 9, 2026 at 9:58 PM CST|Updated: seconds ago

Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google

MOBILE, Ala. (WALA) - Artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of everyday life, raising questions about what the technology could mean for workers and their jobs.

Some economists believe AI poses a particular threat to entry-level and repetitive work, including call center, data entry and junior copywriting jobs, according to The Wall Street Journal. Those tasks may be easier to automate. [...] The long-term impact on jobs remains unclear, but workers can take steps to prepare. Exploring AI chatbots, writing assistants and other tools may help people find ways to work more efficiently and develop skills that complement the technology.

Local training options are available for people who want to learn more. The University of South Alabama offers a hands-on AI workforce training program. The Alabama Community College System also runs workshops, including the AI Community Caravan, that teach foundational AI skills and scam awareness.

Workers can also consider what skills may be valuable in the years ahead, what problems employers may need help solving and how they can become a trusted resource as technology changes.

items.title: IRS official signals additional guidance on AI, practitioner fees
items.summary:
The IRS Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) will issue additional guidance on artificial intelligence (AI) and practitioner fees in the coming months after several organizations, including the AICPA, raised concerns about language in earlier guidance, the agency’s director said Monday at the National Tax Conference.

Thomas Curtin, who noted that he was speaking in his personal capacity and not on behalf of the IRS, said the OPR was “not suggesting that practitioners must reduce fees simply because AI allows you to complete certain tasks more effectively.” [...] Other points discussed during the session included:

 The two warned that taxpayers and practitioners should be cautious about entering tax return information into public AI tools because of potential confidentiality and Sec. 7216 concerns.
 Curtin said AI is not considered a “person” under Circular 230, meaning practitioners cannot rely on AI-generated work in the same way they may rely on the work of another professional.
 Corcoran highlighted concerns about “shadow AI,” in which employees use unapproved AI tools outside firm-approved systems and security controls.
 Corcoran said that many practitioners now receive AI-generated tax analyses from clients and must review those materials using the same professional judgment they apply to other client-provided information. [...] Curtin said the guidance was intended to address transparency and concerns about unconscionable fees, comparing AI to other technologies that have improved efficiency in tax practice, such as tax software and document-scanning tools.

Still, Curtin said that the OPR expects to issue additional guidance on AI and practitioner fees in the next couple of months.

Advertisement

Panelist Ryan Corcoran, a partner with RSM US LLP, said the economics of AI adoption are more complicated than simply measuring time savings, because firms continue to incur implementation, governance, security, and training costs.

“What time savings?” he asked. “It’s just more volume. It’s a lot more work that’s put into a lot of these things.”

items.title: Opinion: AI cannot replace being human – The Battalion
items.summary:
At what point did getting the assignment done become more important than learning something from it?

I understand the appeal. College is busy. Between classes, jobs, extracurriculars, leadership positions and trying to maintain some semblance of a social life, there are never enough hours in the day. AI makes things easier. It can generate an outline, rewrite a paragraph, summarize a reading or produce an entire essay before you have even finished your Celsius. But convenience does not necessarily facilitate education. [...] There is also something to be said about individuality. AI can generate an argument, imitate a writing style or suggest a creative direction, but our perspectives are developed through our own experiences, disagreements, mistakes and interpretations. The things that make our voices interesting are often the very things that cannot be neatly generated from a prompt. If we constantly rely on the same tools to tell us what to think and how to express it, we risk losing the differences that make our contributions worth hearing in the first place. [...] There is a difference between using a tool to improve your work and allowing that tool to replace the work entirely. If AI constructs your argument, develops your ideas and writes your paper, what exactly are you learning? You might walk away with an assignment worth an A, but did you walk away with the ability to produce that work yourself?

We seem to have forgotten that being bad at something is part of learning how to do it well.

Your first essay might be terrible. Your argument might not make sense. You might spend an embarrassing amount of time trying to articulate an idea that sounded much better in your head. That’s okay. Write the terrible first draft. Cross out entire paragraphs. Rewrite your introduction five times.

items.summary:
Những thay đổi trên diễn ra trong bối cảnh quan hệ Việt Nam-Nhật Bản được nng cấp lên Đối tác Chiến lược toàn diện vào tháng 11/2023. Khoa học-công nghệ, đổi mới sáng tạo và chuyển đổi số là những lĩnh vực được hai nước quan tm thúc đẩy hợp tác.

Trong các cuộc trao đổi cấp cao những năm gần đy, AI, bán dẫn, công nghệ lượng tử và đào tạo nhn lực chất lượng cao tiếp tục được đề cập như những hướng hợp tác quan trọng. [...] Đối với Việt Nam, hợp tác với Nhật Bản không chỉ tạo thêm thị trường cho doanh nghiệp công nghệ mà còn mở ra cơ hội tiếp cận các tiêu chuẩn kỹ thuật, phương thức quản trị và quy trình phát triển sản phẩm trong những ngành công nghiệp có yêu cầu cao.

Thêm nữa, nguồn nhn lực công nghệ và khả năng triển khai dịch vụ của doanh nghiệp Việt Nam có thể góp phần đáp ứng một phần nhu cầu chuyển đổi số và hiện đại hóa hệ thống của Nhật Bản. [...] Hơn 15.000 nhn sự trên toàn cầu của FPT đang tham gia hỗ trợ các dự án cho khách hàng Nhật Bản. Hoạt động của doanh nghiệp đã mở rộng từ dịch vụ công nghệ thông tin sang AI, dữ liệu, điện toán đám my, hiện đại hóa các hệ thống công nghệ cũ, công nghệ ô-tô và bán dẫn.

Không chỉ FPT, nhiều doanh nghiệp công nghệ Việt Nam khác cũng từng bước mở rộng hiện diện trực tiếp tại Nhật Bản.

# AI and your job: Threat or opportunity?

Artificial intelligence is changing the workplace. Learn how it could affect jobs and where to find AI training in Alabama.

By Lenise Ligon

Published: Nov. 9, 2026 at 9:58 PM CST|Updated: seconds ago

Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google

MOBILE, Ala. (WALA) - Artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of everyday life, raising questions about what the technology could mean for workers and their jobs.

Some economists believe AI poses a particular threat to entry-level and repetitive work, including call center, data entry and junior copywriting jobs, according to The Wall Street Journal. Those tasks may be easier to automate. [...] The long-term impact on jobs remains unclear, but workers can take steps to prepare. Exploring AI chatbots, writing assistants and other tools may help people find ways to work more efficiently and develop skills that complement the technology.

Local training options are available for people who want to learn more. The University of South Alabama offers a hands-on AI workforce training program. The Alabama Community College System also runs workshops, including the AI Community Caravan, that teach foundational AI skills and scam awareness.

Workers can also consider what skills may be valuable in the years ahead, what problems employers may need help solving and how they can become a trusted resource as technology changes.

items.title: IRS official signals additional guidance on AI, practitioner fees
items.summary:
The IRS Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) will issue additional guidance on artificial intelligence (AI) and practitioner fees in the coming months after several organizations, including the AICPA, raised concerns about language in earlier guidance, the agency’s director said Monday at the National Tax Conference.

Thomas Curtin, who noted that he was speaking in his personal capacity and not on behalf of the IRS, said the OPR was “not suggesting that practitioners must reduce fees simply because AI allows you to complete certain tasks more effectively.” [...] Other points discussed during the session included:

 The two warned that taxpayers and practitioners should be cautious about entering tax return information into public AI tools because of potential confidentiality and Sec. 7216 concerns.
 Curtin said AI is not considered a “person” under Circular 230, meaning practitioners cannot rely on AI-generated work in the same way they may rely on the work of another professional.
 Corcoran highlighted concerns about “shadow AI,” in which employees use unapproved AI tools outside firm-approved systems and security controls.
 Corcoran said that many practitioners now receive AI-generated tax analyses from clients and must review those materials using the same professional judgment they apply to other client-provided information. [...] Curtin said the guidance was intended to address transparency and concerns about unconscionable fees, comparing AI to other technologies that have improved efficiency in tax practice, such as tax software and document-scanning tools.

Still, Curtin said that the OPR expects to issue additional guidance on AI and practitioner fees in the next couple of months.

Panelist Ryan Corcoran, a partner with RSM US LLP, said the economics of AI adoption are more complicated than simply measuring time savings, because firms continue to incur implementation, governance, security, and training costs.

“What time savings?” he asked. “It’s just more volume. It’s a lot more work that’s put into a lot of these things.”

items.title: Opinion: AI cannot replace being human – The Battalion
items.summary:
At what point did getting the assignment done become more important than learning something from it?

I understand the appeal. College is busy. Between classes, jobs, extracurriculars, leadership positions and trying to maintain some semblance of a social life, there are never enough hours in the day. AI makes things easier. It can generate an outline, rewrite a paragraph, summarize a reading or produce an entire essay before you have even finished your Celsius. But convenience does not necessarily facilitate education. [...] There is also something to be said about individuality. AI can generate an argument, imitate a writing style or suggest a creative direction, but our perspectives are developed through our own experiences, disagreements, mistakes and interpretations. The things that make our voices interesting are often the very things that cannot be neatly generated from a prompt. If we constantly rely on the same tools to tell us what to think and how to express it, we risk losing the differences that make our contributions worth hearing in the first place. [...] There is a difference between using a tool to improve your work and allowing that tool to replace the work entirely. If AI constructs your argument, develops your ideas and writes your paper, what exactly are you learning? You might walk away with an assignment worth an A, but did you walk away with the ability to produce that work yourself?

We seem to have forgotten that being bad at something is part of learning how to do it well.

Your first essay might be terrible. Your argument might not make sense. You might spend an embarrassing amount of time trying to articulate an idea that sounded much better in your head. That’s okay. Write the terrible first draft. Cross out entire paragraphs. Rewrite your introduction five times.

The model can also be used to investigate animal sounds through natural-language prompts, potentially making it easier for researchers to analyse recordings in minutes instead of months.

In one test using recordings from Australia's FrogID project, a nation-wide conservation project, NatureLM-audio achieved 99% accuracy in distinguishing frog sounds from other recordings and 82% accuracy in identifying selected frog species. One organisation working at the forefront of this research is the Earth Species Project, a US-based non-profit group developing AI models to analyse animal vocalisations and identify patterns that could help explain how different species communicate.

items.title: Recent advances in AI are creating a 'paradigm shift' for robotics - Berkeley News
items.summary: Traditionally, engineers can directly program the software that tells robots how to perceive objects, plan movements and control their actions, a process called model-based robotics. Or, with model-free robotics, they can train robots to learn behaviors from demonstrations through imitation learning. The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] “Robots are advancing quickly, but developing them for real-world environments remains slow, data-intensive and difficult to scale,” Huang said. “Working with UC Berkeley, NVIDIA is helping advance a new approach combining agentic AI, simulation and open industrial task-focused benchmarks to help developers rapidly test and improve robot behavior before deployment.” [...] Earlier this year, he and his team began experimenting with a change to the way the robot code is organized. Using a framework they called Graph-as-Policy, robot tasks are segmented into individual skills, such as finding an object, planning a grasp and moving the gripper without collisions. Goldberg likened it to individual building blocks that fit together into something much larger.

items.title: OpenAI employees warned about operational security lapses for years, sources say | Reuters
items.summary:
Even before OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022, some company staffers raised concerns internally about its security practices, according to five people familiar with the matter. Employees shared their concerns with top OpenAI leaders ​and the board of directors, the people said, adding that some staffers came away from those interactions concluding that management was more focused on keeping pace with competitors like Google and Anthropic than on security. [...] Another issue is that OpenAI had not done regular security reviews of its internal tools, such as the so-called sandboxes where researchers stress-test new models, three people familiar with the company’s practices said. Employees often modified those tools for their work, but those changes were not always tested for security problems, leaving them potentially vulnerable to attacks from outsiders, the three people said. [...] OpenAI and Anthropic have tried to ​maintain a more open research culture to both ⁠attract employees and foster creativity that can lead to breakthroughs. The AI field is rooted in academia, where machine-learning scientists have openly discussed their research.

Some OpenAI employees are increasingly worried about this approach as AI grows more capable, according to the five people.
